Corresponding method for a wireless communication device, arrangements, access point, wireless communication device and computer program products are also disclosed.

# Method for Managing Wireless Communications Across Multiple Sub-Bands with Differentiated Latency Requirements

## Overview

The disclosed method enables an access point to communicate with multiple wireless communication devices over a frequency bandwidth that is composed of one or more sub-bands. This approach provides a flexible framework for managing access to available spectrum resources while accommodating devices with differing performance needs.

## Device Latency Classifications and Access Mechanism

Within this system, each wireless communication device operates under one of two distinct latency requirements: a first, lower latency requirement or a second, higher latency requirement. This distinction allows the method to differentiate between devices that require rapid, time-sensitive communication and those that can tolerate greater delay.

To gain access to a given sub-band, each device employs a listen-before-talk approach, such as Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA). By sensing the channel before transmitting, devices reduce the likelihood of collisions and contribute to more efficient and orderly use of the shared medium.

## Sub-Band Access Rules

For each sub-band, the method imposes specific rules governing which devices may attempt access. At most one device operating under the first (lower) latency requirement is permitted to attempt access to any given sub-band. Alongside this single low-latency device, one or more devices operating under the second (higher) latency requirement may also contend for access to the same sub-band. This arrangement ensures that latency-sensitive traffic is not subjected to contention from multiple competing low-latency devices, thereby preserving the performance guarantees required by such devices.

## Enforcement of Maximum Transmission Duration

A key aspect of the method is the enforcement of a maximum transmission duration for second-latency devices that share a sub-band with a first-latency device. This maximum transmission duration is determined based on the first latency requirement. By limiting how long the higher-latency devices may occupy the channel, the method ensures that the lower-latency device is able to access the sub-band within a timeframe consistent with its stringent latency needs. In this way, the coexistence of both device types on a single sub-band is achieved without compromising the time-sensitive requirements of the first-latency device.

## Scope of the Disclosure

In addition to the method described above, corresponding methods, arrangements, devices, and computer program products are also disclosed. These are provided for both the access point and the wireless communication devices, ensuring that the complete system can be implemented across all relevant network entities.

# Access Point Method for Managing Wireless Devices with Differentiated Latency Requirements

## Technical Field

This disclosure relates to wireless communication systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for managing access to shared frequency spectrum among wireless communication devices operating under differing latency requirements.

## Background

In modern wireless networks, an access point often serves a heterogeneous population of devices. Some of these devices carry latency-sensitive traffic—such as real-time control signals, industrial automation data, or interactive media—that must be delivered within strict timing constraints. Other devices carry more delay-tolerant traffic, such as bulk data transfers or background updates, which can accommodate longer and more variable latency.

Coordinating access to shared spectrum among these different classes of devices presents a significant challenge. Contention-based access mechanisms, such as listen-before-talk (LBT) protocols including Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA), allow devices to share a channel by sensing whether it is busy before transmitting. However, when multiple low-latency devices contend within the same frequency sub-band, the resulting contention and potential collisions can cause any individual low-latency device to miss its timing requirements. Conversely, excluding higher-latency devices entirely wastes valuable spectrum resources that could otherwise be used productively.

## Summary of the Disclosure

This disclosure describes an access point method for managing wireless communication devices that operate under different latency requirements across multiple frequency sub-bands. The method employs a listen-before-talk approach, such as CSMA/CA, to govern how devices contend for and gain access to the shared spectrum.

According to the method, the access point limits access within any given frequency sub-band to at most one low-latency device. By restricting each sub-band to a single low-latency device, the method eliminates contention among low-latency devices for that sub-band, thereby ensuring that the low-latency device is not delayed by competing low-latency traffic. At the same time, the method permits additional higher-latency devices to contend for access within the same sub-band, allowing the spectrum to be shared efficiently rather than being reserved exclusively for the low-latency device.

## Key Feature: Maximum Transmission Duration for Higher-Latency Devices

A central feature of the method is the enforcement of a maximum transmission duration for the higher-latency devices contending within a given sub-band. This maximum transmission duration is derived from, or based upon, the latency requirement of the low-latency device operating in that sub-band.

By capping the length of any transmission by a higher-latency device, the method guarantees that the channel will not remain occupied by higher-latency traffic for longer than the low-latency device can tolerate. In other words, even if a higher-latency device seizes the channel through the contention process, it must relinquish the channel within a bounded interval. This bounded interval is chosen so that, once the higher-latency transmission concludes, the low-latency device will still be able to access the channel and complete its own transmission within its required timing constraints.

## Operation

In operation, the access point may associate each low-latency device with a respective frequency sub-band and ensure that no two low-latency devices share the same sub-band. Higher-latency devices are then permitted to contend for access across one or more of these sub-bands using the listen-before-talk mechanism. Before or during operation, the access point determines the latency requirement associated with the low-latency device in each sub-band and computes a corresponding maximum transmission duration for higher-latency traffic in that sub-band.

When a higher-latency device wins contention and begins transmitting, its transmission is constrained not to exceed the computed maximum duration. As a result, the low-latency device is assured a bounded worst-case waiting time before it can transmit, satisfying its latency requirement. Meanwhile, the higher-latency device is still able to transmit useful data during the intervals when the low-latency device does not require the channel, achieving efficient utilization of the available spectrum.

## Advantages

The disclosed method provides several advantages. First, by limiting each sub-band to a single low-latency device, it removes a major source of contention-induced delay for latency-sensitive traffic. Second, by permitting higher-latency devices to continue contending within the same sub-band, it avoids wasting spectrum and improves overall channel efficiency. Third, by enforcing a maximum transmission duration tied to the low-latency requirement, it provides a deterministic bound on the delay experienced by low-latency devices, thereby reconciling the competing goals of strict latency guarantees and efficient spectrum sharing.

In this way, the method enables an access point to support a mix of low-latency and higher-latency devices across multiple frequency sub-bands while ensuring that low-latency devices reliably meet their timing constraints and that higher-latency traffic continues to make productive use of the shared spectrum.

# Understanding CSMA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access)

The world of computer networking relies on protocols that allow multiple devices to share a common communication medium without constant interference. One of the foundational protocols developed for this purpose is CSMA, which stands for Carrier Sense Multiple Access. The protocol governs how devices on a shared network determine when it is safe to transmit data.

## How CSMA Works

The core principle behind CSMA is simple yet effective: before a device sends data, it first "listens" to the network to check whether the channel is already in use. This process is known as carrier sensing. The device only proceeds with transmission if it detects that the medium is free, thereby reducing the likelihood of data collisions.

Each device connected to the network follows the same set of rules. Each one must sense the carrier signal, evaluate the state of the channel, and make a decision about transmission independently. This decentralized approach means that no single controller manages access; instead, each node acts based on its own observations of the network environment.

## Variations of the Protocol

The CSMA protocol comes in several important variations:

- **CSMA/CD (Collision Detection):** The device continues to monitor the channel while transmitting, allowing it to detect collisions and stop sending immediately. This variant was widely used in traditional Ethernet networks.

- **CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance):** The protocol takes proactive steps to avoid collisions before they occur, making it especially useful in wireless networks like Wi-Fi.

Each variation addresses specific challenges depending on the type of network and its physical characteristics.

## Why CSMA Matters

The significance of CSMA lies in its ability to coordinate shared resources efficiently. Each transmission attempt is managed in a way that balances fairness and performance across all connected devices. The result is a more orderly and reliable communication system, which remains a cornerstone concept in the study of modern networking.

# Patent Abstract

**Method for Managing Channel Access for Wireless Devices with Different Latency Requirements Over Multiple Sub-Bands Using CSMA/CA**

A method is disclosed for managing channel access by an access point (AP) serving a plurality of wireless devices having heterogeneous latency requirements across a plurality of frequency sub-bands. The access point partitions an available operating bandwidth into multiple sub-bands and classifies associated wireless devices into latency categories based on their respective latency requirements, such as low-latency and latency-tolerant traffic classes. The method comprises assigning one or more sub-bands to each latency category and applying a Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA) protocol independently on each sub-band, wherein contention parameters—including contention window sizes, interframe spacing, and backoff intervals—are configured according to the latency requirements associated with the respective sub-band. The access point performs clear channel assessment on each sub-band and coordinates channel access such that low-latency devices contend on sub-bands configured with reduced contention parameters to minimize access delay, while latency-tolerant devices contend on sub-bands configured for improved spectral efficiency and throughput. In some embodiments, the access point dynamically reallocates sub-bands and adjusts contention parameters in response to changing traffic loads, channel conditions, or quality-of-service demands. The method enables differentiated channel access that satisfies diverse latency constraints while maintaining efficient utilization of the shared wireless medium.

# ABSTRACT

A wireless access point and methods for coordinating heterogeneous client devices operating across shared frequency sub-bands using listen-before-talk (LBT) channel access. The access point classifies associated wireless devices into at least a low-latency traffic class and a high-latency traffic class based on quality-of-service requirements, application signaling, or traffic pattern analysis. A frequency band is partitioned into a plurality of sub-bands, and the access point dynamically allocates sub-bands to the respective device classes according to real-time latency demands and channel occupancy. To reduce medium contention for delay-sensitive traffic, the access point applies differentiated LBT parameters to each sub-band, including class-dependent clear-channel-assessment thresholds, contention window sizes, backoff durations, and channel-sensing intervals, thereby granting low-latency devices statistically prioritized access to designated sub-bands while high-latency devices contend on remaining sub-bands. In some embodiments, the access point transmits control signaling that reserves or schedules sub-band access opportunities, coordinates cross-sub-band aggregation when channels are idle, and reallocates sub-bands between classes in response to changing load conditions. The disclosed techniques improve latency bounds and channel utilization for mixed-criticality workloads while maintaining fair coexistence with other network devices sharing unlicensed or shared spectrum.

# Patent-Style Summary: Managing Multi-Latency Device Access in a Wireless Network

## Abstract

A method and system for managing wireless medium access among devices having differing latency requirements. An access point regulates the number of low-latency devices permitted to access a designated sub-band while concurrently enforcing transmission duration constraints upon high-latency devices, thereby optimizing spectral utilization and preserving latency guarantees for time-sensitive traffic.

---

## Summary of the Invention

In one aspect, the present disclosure describes a method performed by an access point (AP) operating in a wireless communication network. The method comprises:

**(a)** designating at least one sub-band of an available frequency spectrum for preferential use by low-latency devices;

**(b)** determining, by the access point, an admission threshold specifying a maximum number of low-latency devices permitted to concurrently access the designated sub-band;

**(c)** receiving access requests from a plurality of wireless devices, each device being classified according to a latency characteristic as either a low-latency device or a high-latency device;

**(d)** admitting low-latency devices to the designated sub-band up to the admission threshold, and selectively denying or redirecting access requests from additional low-latency devices when the admission threshold is reached; and

**(e)** for high-latency devices accessing the network, enforcing a transmission duration limit that constrains the maximum contiguous time each such device may occupy the wireless medium during a given transmission opportunity.

In a further aspect, the transmission duration limit imposed upon high-latency devices is dynamically adjusted by the access point based on one or more of: current channel occupancy, the number of admitted low-latency devices, aggregate traffic load, and quality-of-service (QoS) requirements associated with pending low-latency traffic.

In another aspect, the access point transmits control signaling to the wireless devices indicating at least one of: the admission threshold, an assignment to the designated sub-band, and the applicable transmission duration limit.

In yet a further aspect, enforcement of the transmission duration limit comprises the access point causing a high-latency device to cease transmission upon expiration of the duration limit, thereby creating transmission gaps during which latency-sensitive traffic from admitted low-latency devices may be serviced.

---

## Illustrative Claim Language

**Claim 1.** A method for wireless medium management, comprising:
- designating, by an access point, a sub-band for low-latency communication;
- limiting a number of low-latency devices granted access to the sub-band to a predetermined admission threshold; and
- enforcing, upon one or more high-latency devices, a maximum transmission duration limiting occupancy of the wireless medium per transmission opportunity.

**Claim 2.** The method of Claim 1, wherein the admission threshold is determined based on an aggregate latency budget of the sub-band.

**Claim 3.** The method of Claim 1, further comprising dynamically modifying the maximum transmission duration in response to changing network conditions.

---

*Would you like me to expand this into additional independent and dependent claims, add a detailed description of a preferred embodiment, or include figure descriptions (e.g., flowcharts or system diagrams)?*

# Abstract

A method and system for scheduling wireless communication devices operating under two distinct latency requirements in a shared wireless network. The scheduling framework categorizes devices into a first latency class associated with a first maximum transmission duration and a second latency class associated with a second maximum transmission duration, wherein the second maximum transmission duration is shorter than the first maximum transmission duration to accommodate low-latency traffic. A scheduler allocates frequency resources across a plurality of sub-bands according to sub-band access rules that reserve or prioritize designated sub-bands for devices of the second latency class, thereby reducing queuing and preemption delays for latency-sensitive transmissions. Devices of the first latency class are constrained to transmissions not exceeding the first maximum transmission duration and are permitted access to sub-bands not currently reserved for the second latency class. In some embodiments, the sub-band access rules dynamically adjust sub-band assignments based on traffic load, channel conditions, or quality-of-service indicators, and support preemption of ongoing first-class transmissions to satisfy second-class latency constraints. The disclosed techniques improve spectral efficiency while ensuring that heterogeneous devices meet their respective latency requirements within the same wireless communication system.

# ABSTRACT

A method performed by an access point for managing latency-differentiated channel access in a wireless communication network is disclosed. The access point classifies wireless devices, or traffic associated therewith, into a plurality of latency categories, each latency category being associated with a respective set of channel access parameters governing contention-based access to a shared wireless medium. The access point transmits, to one or more wireless devices, control signaling indicative of the channel access parameters corresponding to the latency category assigned to each respective wireless device, thereby enabling differentiated medium access whereby latency-sensitive traffic is afforded prioritized channel access relative to latency-tolerant traffic.

A corresponding method performed by a wireless device comprises receiving the control signaling from the access point, determining the set of channel access parameters associated with a latency category applicable to the wireless device or its traffic, and contending for access to the shared wireless medium in accordance with the determined channel access parameters.

Corresponding arrangements are also disclosed, including an access point and a wireless device, each comprising processing circuitry and memory configured to carry out the respective methods. The processing circuitry may be operatively coupled to communication interface circuitry for transmitting and receiving signaling over the wireless medium.

Further disclosed are computer program products comprising a non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions which, when executed by processing circuitry of an access point or a wireless device, cause the respective apparatus to perform the methods described herein.

The disclosed techniques enable improved differentiation of channel access based on latency requirements, thereby enhancing quality of service, reducing latency for time-critical applications, and improving overall utilization of the shared wireless medium.
